sections.h2: Where is the Lebanon County Recorder of Deeds, and when is it open?
sections.html:
The Recorder of Deeds in Lebanon County works from Room 107 of the Municipal Building at 400 South 8th Street in the city of Lebanon, PA 17042. The office answers questions at 717-228-4447 and keeps weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Everything that touches title to land in the county gets filed here: deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, easements, plans, and also UCC financing filings and notary bonds. For a seller, that means two trips through this office. The deed from the old owner to you was recorded here when you bought, and the deed you sign at closing goes onto the same record. If a mortgage is being paid off from your sale proceeds, the lender's satisfaction piece also lands on the county record, usually a few weeks after the payoff.

The staff will help you find a record, but they will not tell you how to word a deed or whether a name should come off one. Their own FAQ says the office is a custodian of records and sends those questions to an attorney.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a deed in Lebanon County?
sections.html:
A standard deed or mortgage costs $91.75 to record under the fee schedule that took effect November 12, 2025. That base price covers up to four pages and four names, and it already contains the affordable housing fee, the records improvement fee, the parcel identifier fee and the court and access-to-justice surcharges, so those do not show up as separate line items.

A few smaller charges can matter on a sale:

  • A Statement of Value that has attachments adds $2.00 for each attachment page. The duplicate copy for the state carries no charge.
  • Sending a document by email to the office costs $5.00 plus $0.50 for each page.
  • A returned check costs $30.00.
  • Copies run $0.50 per page up to 11 by 17 inches, and oversized pages add $5.00.

The office takes cash or checks only. Make the check payable to the Recorder of Deeds for the exact amount, since the office states that fees and transfer taxes are due at the time of recording.

sections.h2: What does a Lebanon County deed need before the office will record it?
sections.html:
The deed must show a Uniform Parcel Identifier, called a UPI, on its first page, and that number must be certified by the county Assessment Office. The certification happens electronically inside the courthouse. If you do not have the number, call Assessment at 717-228-4425 or use the county property viewer to look the parcel up by address.

The county's recording instructions add several other requirements:

  • A signed certificate of residence for the grantee on every deed, and for the mortgagee on every mortgage or assignment.
  • Type no smaller than 10 point, and a legal acknowledgment before a notary.
  • A typed English translation attached to any document written in another language.
  • Page numbers or numbering that shows the filing order when several documents belong to one transaction.
  • For land that sits in more than one municipality or school district, the share of the property in each one, stated as a percentage so the local transfer tax can be divided.
  • A self-addressed stamped envelope large enough for the return of the originals.

A Statement of Value, the state's REV-183 form, is filed in duplicate with its attachments. It is required when the deed does not state the full price, when the transfer is a gift or has no consideration, when an exemption is claimed, and when the property was sold at a tax claim or sheriff sale. The county notes that a statement is not needed when full consideration is paid, when the transfer is between close family members, or when the grant is an easement to a public utility. Fill in every block, sign it, and date it with the settlement or acceptance date.

sections.h2: How much realty transfer tax is due on a Lebanon County sale?
sections.html:
Pennsylvania charges a 1 percent state realty transfer tax on the value of the property, and the Recorder of Deeds collects it at the counter when the deed is recorded. The Department of Revenue states that the grantor and the grantee are both liable for it. Local transfer tax is collected on top of the state amount and is shared by the school district and municipality where the house stands. Ask the Recorder of Deeds, or your closing agent, for the combined rate that applies to your street address.

Some transfers are exempt, including certain transfers between family members, transfers by will or intestate succession, and transfers to government bodies. The county points claimants to the state's exemption rules and wants the REV-183 to explain the basis. The county FAQ also gives Lebanon County's assessed ratio, known as the common level ratio, as 1.39 percent that also appears on the Statement of Value.

In a typical sale the title company or attorney works out the tax and brings a check to the office. How the cost is divided between buyer and seller is a term of the purchase agreement.

sections.h2: How long does recording take, and can I record electronically?
sections.html:
The county says most documents come back the next business day, by pickup, mail or electronic return, whichever the submitter chose. Each document is received, reviewed and keyed in, sent to Assessment to certify the UPI, returned for recording, and then proofread. Documents are recorded in the order they arrive, so a heavy day can lengthen the wait.

Electronic recording is accepted through Simplifile, CSC and ePN, three vendors the office lists by name, and confirmation can come back in minutes. If you file by mail, include a check for the exact amount and the return envelope.

Landex, the county's records vendor, also runs record alerts tied to a parcel number. Owners of a rental house or of a home left empty after an inheritance may want to ask the Recorder of Deeds how to sign up.

sections.h2: How do I look up deeds and mortgages recorded in Lebanon County?
sections.html:
Lebanon County was established in 1813, and its recorded documents from 1925 to the present can be searched online through Landex. Anything older has to be viewed at the office in Room 107. The records are open to the public, with one exception: military discharge papers (DD214 forms) are kept private. Veterans can record a DD214 for free and may get a Veterans ID Card.

Phone help is limited, because the office is not insured for title searching. Plan to do your own search online, or hire a title company if the chain of ownership is complicated. A deed describes the land and not the buildings on it, so adding a house to a lot does not produce a new deed.

Notary commissions are handled in the same office. The notary fee is $42.00, which includes the Prothonotary fee, paid by one check payable to the Recorder of Deeds.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Lebanon County itself?
sections.html:
Lebanon County covers 362 square miles in south central Pennsylvania, about 72 miles northwest of Philadelphia. It was cut from Dauphin and Lancaster counties in 1813, and the city of Lebanon is the county seat and its largest community. The 2020 census counted 143,257 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 146,380.

Swatara Creek drains most of the valley toward the Susquehanna, while Tulpehocken Creek near Myerstown runs east toward the Schuylkill. Interstates 78, 81 and the Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-76) cross the county, along with US 22, 322 and 422. Dauphin, Lancaster, Berks and Schuylkill counties border it.

  • Larger communities by 2010 count: Lebanon, Palmyra, Cornwall, Myerstown and Cleona.
  • Colleges: Lebanon Valley College, Evangelical Seminary and the Lebanon campus of Harrisburg Area Community College.
  • Climate: hot, humid summers and cold winters, with city averages from about 29 degrees in January to about 74 in July.

Whether a house sits in Lebanon city, a borough such as Palmyra, or a township changes which municipality and school district receive the local transfer tax, so confirm your municipality before you estimate closing costs.

faqs.q: What is the fee to record a deed in Lebanon County?
faqs.a: The base fee is $91.75 for up to four pages and four names, under the schedule effective November 12, 2025. Each extra page costs $4.00 and each extra name $1.00. The county accepts cash or check only.

faqs.q: Does Lebanon County require a parcel number on a deed?
faqs.a: Yes. The Uniform Parcel Identifier must appear on the first page and be certified by the Assessment Office. Call 717-228-4425 to get the number for your property.

faqs.q: Can I record a Lebanon County deed by email or mail?
faqs.a: Mail works if you include the exact fee by check and a stamped return envelope. Email submission is accepted for $5.00 plus $0.50 per page, and electronic recording through Simplifile, CSC or ePN is also available.

faqs.q: How soon will my recorded deed come back?
faqs.a: Most documents are returned the next business day. The wait depends on how many documents were filed ahead of yours, since the office records in order of arrival.

faqs.q: Who pays the realty transfer tax in Lebanon County?
faqs.a: Both the seller and the buyer are legally liable to the state, and the tax is due when the deed is recorded. Who bears the cost in practice is set by the sales contract, so check it with your closing agent.
